problem.p: Thermal bridging occurs wherever a material of high thermal conductivity penetrates the insulated layer of a building envelope. A steel stud crossing a wall cavity, a concrete slab edge meeting an exterior wall, or a balcony cantilevered through the insulation line all create a preferential path for heat flow. The consequence is measurable: the effective R-value of the assembly drops well below the nominal value printed on the insulation packaging, and the interior surface temperature at the bridge falls closer to the outdoor temperature than the designer intended.

Two failure modes follow. The first is energy loss, which appears directly in heating and cooling bills. The second, and more damaging, is surface condensation: when the interior surface at the bridge drops below the dew point of the indoor air, moisture accumulates, and sustained moisture in a wall assembly leads to mould growth and eventual material degradation. A designer who accounts only for the first has solved the cheaper half of the problem.

Consider a wall assembly with nominal insulation of R-20, framed with steel studs at 400 mm on centre. The steel conducts roughly 400 times more heat than the mineral wool between the studs, so although the studs occupy a small fraction of the wall area, they carry a disproportionate share of the heat flow. Measurements of such assemblies routinely show effective values near R-11 — barely more than half the nominal figure. Substituting wood studs, which conduct far less, recovers much of the loss. Placing a continuous layer of exterior insulation outboard of the framing recovers more still, because it interrupts every bridge at once rather than treating them one at a time.

ul.li: Conduction moves heat through solid material in contact.
Convection moves heat by the bulk motion of air or water.
Radiation moves heat between surfaces with no medium required.
A thermal bridge short-circuits the first of these three.

problem.p: An engineer from the American Society of Heating, Refrigerating and Air-Conditioning Engineers (ASHRAE) would describe the retrofit above as moving the assembly from a bridged condition to a continuously insulated one. The distinction matters for code compliance, because prescriptive paths in most energy codes now specify continuous insulation explicitly rather than relying on nominal cavity values alone.

Quantifying a bridge begins with the linear thermal transmittance, written as psi and expressed in watts per metre kelvin. Unlike the U-value of a plane assembly, psi describes the additional heat flow attributable to the detail itself, over and above what the adjacent assemblies already lose. A slab edge with a psi of 0.9 W/m·K running the full perimeter of a floor plate contributes more to the building's heat loss than most designers estimate from intuition, and the contribution grows in proportion to the building's form factor.

Field verification matters because modelled details and built details diverge. Insulation is compressed where a contractor forced it past a bracket; a membrane is lapped the wrong way at a corner; a service penetration drilled after the fact is never resealed. An infrared survey conducted with a sufficient temperature difference across the envelope, at least ten degrees Celsius, reveals these departures in minutes. The survey is diagnostic rather than quantitative: it tells you where to look, not how much heat is escaping, so it pairs naturally with a blower door test and targeted heat flux measurements.

Remediation strategy depends on whether the bridge repeats. Repeating linear bridges, such as studs or joists, are best addressed by adding a continuous layer that crosses all of them. Isolated bridges, such as a single structural column landing on a slab, may justify a bespoke detail: a structural thermal break, a load-bearing insulating block engineered to carry compression while conducting far less than steel or concrete. These components cost considerably more per unit than insulation board, which is why identifying whether a bridge repeats is the first question to answer.

Finally, a caution about nominal figures. Marketing literature quotes the R-value of a product in isolation, measured through the material with no fasteners, no framing and no gaps. The number a building actually achieves is the effective R-value of the assembly as built, and the gap between the two is precisely the subject of this unit. A designer who specifies R-20 and delivers R-11 has not made an arithmetic error; they have omitted the bridges from the calculation.

multiplechoiceresponse.label: Which change to the wall assembly described above will reduce thermal bridging the most?

choicegroup.choice: Increasing the depth of the cavity insulation between the existing steel studs.
Adding a continuous layer of rigid insulation outboard of the steel framing.
Sealing every penetration in the interior vapour barrier with tape.
Replacing the interior gypsum board with a thicker, denser panel.

solution.p: Continuous exterior insulation interrupts every bridge at once, which is why it outperforms any change confined to the cavity. Deeper cavity insulation still leaves the studs conducting straight through the assembly, and neither air sealing nor a heavier interior finish changes the conductive path.
